blocks.content: When your code encounters something it cannot handle a file that doesn't exist, a network that dropped, a number divided by zero it throws an exception. But not all exceptions are equal. Some demand that you acknowledge them at compile time.
Others fly past silently until they crash your program at runtime. Understanding the difference is one of the most important judgment calls in software design.
This lesson covers what checked and unchecked exceptions are, how the three major languages handle them, when to use each, and the mistakes that show up most often in real codebases.

blocks.content: 1. The core idea
A checked exception is one the compiler forces you to deal with. You must either catch it or declare that your method might throw it.
An unchecked exception is one the compiler ignores it may or may not be caught, and the program only finds out at runtime if something goes wrong.
Think of it this way: checked exceptions say "this failure is expected and you must plan for it." Unchecked exceptions say "this failure represents a bug or an environment you cannot recover from."
Java exception hierarchy only Java has a formal compiler-enforced checked/unchecked split
2. Checked exceptions

A checked exception must be handled at compile time. The compiler refuses to build your program if you call a method that declares it throws a checked exception and you neither catch it nor re-declare it in your own method's signature.
The intent is good: it forces the caller to think about failure modes they would otherwise forget.

Java is the only mainstream language with compiler-enforced checked exceptions. C++ and Python treat every exception as unchecked catching is always optional, and only documentation or testing reveals what a function might throw.
3. Unchecked exceptions
An unchecked exception is one the compiler does not require you to handle. It propagates up the call stack until something catches it, or it crashes the program.
These typically represent programming mistakes accessing a null reference, going out of array bounds, dividing by zero where recovery at the call site rarely makes sense.
4. Catching and re-throwing

Catching an exception lets you react to the failure log it, clean up resources, return a fallback, or wrap it in a higher-level exception that makes more sense to the caller. Re-throwing means you handle what you can and let the rest propagate.
The pattern of catching a low-level exception and re-throwing a domain-specific one is called exception translation.
The caller of PaymentService should not have to know that the failure was an IOException at the file layer it only needs to know the payment failed and why.
Wrapping preserves the original cause for logging and debugging while keeping the API clean.
5. Creating custom exceptions

Custom exceptions let you name failures in terms that make sense for your domain rather than leaking implementation details to callers. In Java you choose whether to make them checked or unchecked by which class you extend.

blocks.content: 9. Common mistakes

Mistake 1: empty catch block Catching an exception and doing nothing with it is worse than not catching it at all. The failure disappears silently and the bug becomes invisible until it causes a much harder-to-trace problem downstream. At minimum, log the exception.

Mistake 2: converting unchecked to checked unnecessarily (Java) Wrapping everyRuntimeExceptionin a checked exception forces every caller up the stack to add try-catch, adding noise without adding safety. If the failure is a programming mistake, leave it unchecked.

Mistake 3: using exceptions for normal control flow Throwing an exception to signal "item not found" or "list is empty" is expensive and misleading. Exceptions are for unexpected failures. Use a return value, anOptional, or a null for expected absence.

Mistake 4: losing the original cause (Python) Writingraise PaymentError("failed")inside an except block discards the original traceback. Useraise PaymentError("failed") from eto chain the cause so it appears in the traceback and can be inspected in production logs.

Mistake 5: not using RAII / try-with-resources for cleanup (C++ / Java) Relying on a try-finally to close a file or release a lock works until an exception is thrown before the finally is reached. C++ destructors and Java'stry-with-resourcesguarantee cleanup regardless of how the block exits.

blocks.content: 11. The debate: were checked exceptions a good idea
blocks.text: 11. The debate: were checked exceptions a good idea

blocks.content: Java shipped checked exceptions in 1996 with a clear goal: force programmers to confront failure instead of ignoring it. Three decades later, the feature is one of the most argued-about design choices in language history, and almost every language designed since has deliberately left it out.
The case against checked exceptions

{"headers":["Argument","Explanation"],"rows":[["Boilerplate without safety","Developers under deadline pressure often add a catch block that only logs and swallows, or a throws clause that just forwards the problem, satisfying the compiler without actually improving reliability"],["Breaks encapsulation across versions","Adding a new checked exception to a method is a source incompatible change, every caller in the codebase must be updated to catch or declare it, which discourages library authors from evolving their error handling later"],["Does not compose with functional interfaces","A checked exception cannot be thrown from inside a standard Java lambda passed to map, filter, or forEach without extra wrapping, which pushes people toward unchecked exceptions purely to keep the code compiling"],["No mainstream successor kept it","C#, Kotlin, Scala, Go, Rust, Python, and JavaScript all shipped after Java and none of them chose to enforce a compiler level checked and unchecked split the way Java does"]]}
The case for checked exceptions

The feature is not without defenders. A checked exception on a public method is a form of documentation the compiler enforces, unlike a comment or a wiki page, it cannot go stale. It also makes a library boundary explicit: anyone integrating a payment gateway or a file parser is told, at compile time, exactly which failures they must plan for before the code ships.

Checked exceptions were meant to make software more reliable by making failure impossible to ignore. In practice, many teams treat them as paperwork to satisfy the compiler, catching and immediately rethrowing without ever truly deciding how to recover.

The honest middle ground most experienced Java teams reach today: use checked exceptions sparingly, at a small number of well chosen boundaries where the caller genuinely needs to make a decision, and let everything else, especially internal bugs, be unchecked.

blocks.content: When you design a system, you are not just choosing between two Java base classes, you are deciding what your API promises to the people who call it. The questions below apply even outside Java, since every language needs a convention for which failures a caller must plan for.
Questions to ask before creating a custom exception

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question","Why it matters"],"rows":[["Can the immediate caller do something useful with this failure","If the answer is retry, show a message, or pick a fallback, the failure is a candidate for a checked, explicitly declared exception"],["Does this represent a bug rather than an external condition","A null where a value was guaranteed, or an index that should have already been validated, is a programming error, not something a caller should be forced to catch"],["Is this a public API boundary or purely internal","Public boundaries benefit from explicit, checked contracts, internal implementation details rarely do"],["Will declaring this exception add real value or just noise","If every caller up the chain will only rethrow it unchanged, forcing a declaration adds boilerplate without adding safety"],["What do the frameworks I already depend on do","Mixing conventions inconsistently, checked here, unchecked there, for the same kind of failure, confuses anyone reading the code later"]]}
Hierarchy design mistakes to avoid

blocks.title: Common pitfalls
blocks.content: Making every exception in a hierarchy checked forces callers at every level to add a try-catch that only rethrows, adding noise without adding safety. Making everything unchecked, including genuinely expected business failures, removes the compiler help entirely and it becomes easy to forget a catch. Building deep hierarchies with a new subclass for every minor variation, when a small number of types with a reason code field would communicate the same information with far less code to maintain. Naming a class so it ends in Exception without documenting whether callers actually need to catch it, the name alone does not tell anyone which category it belongs to.
13. Worked example: an exception hierarchy for a payment processor
blocks.text: 13. Worked example: an exception hierarchy for a payment processor

blocks.content: Consider a payment processor that talks to an external card gateway. Some failures are ordinary parts of doing business, a card gets declined, a refund is attempted twice. Other failures are bugs, an order reaching the charge method with a zero amount should never happen if validation upstream is correct. The hierarchy below keeps those two categories visibly separate.
Requirements for the hierarchy

["Expected business failures, a declined card, an already refunded transaction, a gateway timeout, are checked so every integration point is forced to explicitly decide how to handle them","Programming errors, an order amount that should already be positive, a missing configuration value, are unchecked so they surface immediately during development instead of being silently caught and hidden","All payment specific checked exceptions share one abstract base class, so a single catch block can log and alert on anything payment related if that is ever needed","Each exception carries a structured error code so calling code can branch on the failure type without parsing a free text message"]

blocks.content: How the hierarchy is used in practice
blocks.text: How the hierarchy is used in practice

blocks.content: The abstract PaymentException carries the shared errorCode field and constructor logic, but it is never thrown directly, only its concrete subclasses are. Because CardDeclinedException, PaymentAlreadyRefundedException, and GatewayTimeoutException are all checked, the compiler forces charge to declare throws for each of them, and forces every caller to either catch each one or propagate it further up. InvalidTransactionStateException and PaymentServiceMisconfiguredException, by contrast, need no declaration at all, they are allowed to crash straight through to a global error handler because no caller could have done anything sensible with them anyway.

blocks.title: Tracing one request through the hierarchy
blocks.text: A customer submits an order for 49.99. The gateway responds that the card was declined for insufficient funds. PaymentProcessor.charge throws a checked CardDeclinedException carrying the error code CARD_DECLINED, and because the exception is checked, the calling controller cannot compile unless it decides what to do, so a decline can never be silently dropped on the way to the customer facing response. Now contrast that with a bug where the order total was somehow computed as zero before reaching charge. That should never happen if validation ran correctly, so it throws the unchecked InvalidTransactionStateException, which propagates straight to the on call engineer instead of being caught and quietly retried.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Class","Checked or unchecked","Thrown when"],"rows":[["PaymentException","Checked, abstract base","Never thrown directly, parent for every expected payment failure"],["CardDeclinedException","Checked","The gateway reports that the card was declined"],["PaymentAlreadyRefundedException","Checked","A refund is attempted on a transaction that was already refunded"],["GatewayTimeoutException","Checked","The payment gateway does not respond within the timeout window"],["InvalidTransactionStateException","Unchecked","An order reaches the processor in a state validation should have already prevented"],["PaymentServiceMisconfiguredException","Unchecked","A required configuration value, such as an API key, is missing at startup"]]}

This hierarchy keeps the two concerns visibly separate. Checked subclasses of PaymentException model business outcomes that every caller must plan for: declines, duplicate refunds, timeouts. Unchecked subclasses of RuntimeException model bugs, an amount that should already have been validated, a configuration that should already have been checked, that no caller should be expected to recover from at the point of the call.
